title: Kitesurf now open source – Cloudflare's agentic browser on Dioxus Blitz
content:
Kitesurf is an experimental browser engine that runs on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, runs page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without Chrome or a browser container.
Kitesurf speaks the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can use it with CDP clients such as Puppeteer.
Important
Kitesurf requires Cloudflare Dynamic Workers to create isolated workers for
pages. Dynamic Workers are part of the Workers Paid plan.
Local development uses wrangler dev. A Cloudflare Workers Paid plan is
required to run Kitesurf on Cloudflare.
- Bazelisk, installed as bazel.
Bazel builds everything. It downloads the pinned Bazel, Rust toolchains,
wasm-bindgen, and binaryen itself.
- Node.js 22 or newer
- pnpm 9.15.4, which the repository pins in package.json
- On macOS, GNU tar (brew install gnu-tar)
- Rust through rustup, only for editing the vendored
crate patches. rust-toolchain.toml pins the same nightly that Bazel uses.
Install pnpm separately if it is not already available:
npm install --global pnpm@9.15.4
Clone the repository and install its dependencies:
git clone https://github.com/cloudflare/kitesurf.git
cd kitesurf
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
Build and start the local engine:
pnpm run dev
The engine listens on http://127.0.0.1:8787. Visit
http://127.0.0.1:8787/health to confirm that it is running.
The root URL shows the landing page. It has a form to open a URL in Chrome DevTools, example pages, and the CDP endpoints for agents and other clients. See Use Chrome DevTools.
pnpm run dev builds the WebAssembly modules and the page and renderer bundles
with Bazel, then starts wrangler dev. The first build compiles the Rust core
and its vendored crates, which takes a while; later builds reuse Bazel's cache.
Set KITESURF_PORT when port 8787 is already in use:
KITESURF_PORT=8799 pnpm run dev
Install puppeteer-core in the project that will control Kitesurf. Then connect
to the browser WebSocket endpoint:
import puppeteer from "puppeteer-core";
const browser = await puppeteer.connect({
  browserWSEndpoint: "ws://127.0.0.1:8787/devtools/browser",
});
const page = await browser.newPage();
await page.goto("https://example.com/");
await page.screenshot({ path: "page.png" });
await browser.disconnect();
Use the port from KITESURF_PORT if you selected a different port. HTTP
discovery is available at http://127.0.0.1:8787/json/version.
With pnpm run dev, open http://127.0.0.1:8787/ in Chrome. Enter a URL to
inspect, or select one of the example pages. DevTools opens in the tab on that
page. To go to DevTools directly, open
http://127.0.0.1:8787/?url=https://example.com, or
http://127.0.0.1:8787/?inspect=1 for a blank page.
If you built the bundled frontend, pnpm run dev serves it from the engine's
own origin. See
Use the bundled DevTools frontend.
Otherwise, the DevTools frontend comes from
chrome-devtools-frontend.appspot.com, the build that Google hosts for Chrome.
The hosted frontend has these limits:
- The first time it connects, Chrome asks whether
chrome-devtools-frontend.appspot.com can access apps on this device. Select
Allow.
- If you block this access, DevTools says that the WebSocket disconnected. To allow it again, click the site information icon to the left of the address. Then allow the access and reconnect DevTools.
- The frontend can connect only to 127.0.0.1. Thus it does not work with a
deployed engine.
You can also use chrome://inspect:
- Open chrome://inspect/#devices in Chrome. Type or paste it into the address
bar because web pages cannot link to it.
- Select Discover network targets.
- Select Configure... and add 127.0.0.1:8787.
- Under Remote Target, select inspect next to kitesurf.
- Enter a page URL in the address bar above the screencast.
Use the port from KITESURF_PORT when you select a different local port. Chrome
discovers targets with plain HTTP and WebSocket connections. The chrome://inspect
workflow cannot reach an HTTPS engine. Use it with a local engine instead.
Kitesurf provides a CDP endpoint, not a full Chrome implementation. Some Chrome
DevTools features do not work yet. We are working to add more support over time.
Puppeteer and other CDP clients can connect to
ws://127.0.0.1:8787/devtools/browser.
Kitesurf can serve the Chrome DevTools frontend from its own origin. Then
DevTools works without the hosted frontend, its permission prompt and the
127.0.0.1 limit. A deployed engine always uses this copy. The frontend is the
prebuilt build that Google publishes for Chromium. The default build does not
include it.
The --config=devtools Bazel option adds the frontend to the build. The first
build with it downloads the frontend (about 250 MB). Bazel keeps the download
in its cache for later builds.
To build the frontend once, run this command from the repository root:
bazel run --config=devtools //packages/engine:dev_build
To include the frontend in every local build, add the option to
.bazelrc.user. Git ignores this file. Then pnpm run build and
pnpm run dev include the frontend.
echo 'common --config=devtools' >> .bazelrc.user
The build copies the frontend to packages/engine/public/inspector/. Git
ignores this directory. A build without the option removes it. To turn the
frontend off, remove the line from .bazelrc.user.
- Build the frontend as described above.
- Start the engine with pnpm run dev. The engine serves the bundled frontend
when the build includes it, and the hosted frontend when it does not.
- Open http://127.0.0.1:8787/ in Chrome. Enter a URL to inspect, or select
one of the example pages. DevTools opens in the tab on that page.
To start on a page, open http://127.0.0.1:8787/?url=https://example.com.
Use the smallest step that fixes the problem:
- To copy the frontend files again, delete the copy and build again: rm -rf packages/engine/public/inspector bazel run --config=devtools //packages/engine:dev_build
- To extract the archive again, for example after you change
bazel/devtools_frontend.BUILD, fetch it again and then build:
bazel fetch --force --repo=@devtools_frontend --config=devtools bazel run --config=devtools //packages/engine:dev_build Bazel extracts the archive from its cache. To download the archive again
from Google, add --repository_cache= to the bazel fetch command.
Do not use bazel clean --expunge for this. It also removes the WebAssembly
build and the rest of the Bazel cache.
Two pins select the frontend version:
- DEVTOOLS_FRONTEND_REV and the values after it in MODULE.bazel select the
bundled frontend. The comment above them tells you how to select a new
snapshot.
- KITESURF_INSPECTOR_FALLBACK_URL in the local environment of packages/engine/wrangler.jsonc selects the hosted frontend. Use the
Chrome commit that https://chromiumdash.appspot.com/fetch_version?version=<chrome-version> returns in hashes.chromium.
Keep the two pins on the same Chrome version. After you change
MODULE.bazel, the next build downloads the new archive.
The pnpm scripts are front ends to Bazel:
pnpm run build                    # bazel run //packages/engine:dev_build
pnpm run check                    # type checks, bundles, and repository checks
pnpm run test:unit                # engine vitest and Rust host tests
pnpm run test:e2e <file-substring>
pnpm run format:check             # oxfmt; pnpm run format rewrites the same files
pnpm run format:rust              # format Rust with Bazel's pinned rustfmt
pnpm run lint                     # oxlint, the custom lint rules, and Rust lint
The Rust formatter rewrites tracked and non-ignored untracked files, excluding
paths in .oxfmtrc.json.
pnpm run build copies the Bazel-built WebAssembly, bundles, and RBI files into
the source tree, where wrangler dev reads them. Other targets run directly,
for example bazel test //tests/e2e:gate for the full e2e suite. Another Bazel
workspace can depend on this repository as a module.
Kitesurf combines several open-source Rust projects:
- Blitz provides HTML parsing, the DOM,
layout, and painting. It is licensed under MIT OR Apache-

report.summary: Cloudflare open-sourced Kitesurf, an experimental Rust/WebAssembly browser engine for Workers that renders pages and speaks Chrome DevTools Protocol for agent use.
report.background: AI agents increasingly need to fetch, execute and inspect real web pages, but conventional headless Chrome is heavy: it requires browser binaries, containers, memory and patching, and is awkward to isolate per task at edge scale. Cloudflare has been pushing Workers as a place to run untrusted code close to users, and its Dynamic Workers can spin up isolated per-page runtimes. Kitesurf applies that model to browsing: rather than wrapping Chrome, it implements a small browser engine in Rust/WebAssembly using Dioxus Blitz for HTML parsing, DOM, layout and painting. Speaking Chrome DevTools Protocol is a pragmatic adoption trick: existing Puppeteer and DevTools workflows can drive it. The project is experimental and tied to paid Workers, so it is a signal about serverless agent infrastructure rather than a production Chrome replacement.
key_points: Kitesurf is not a Chrome wrapper. It runs on Cloudflare Workers, parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript and produces screenshots without a browser container. Each page can run in an isolated Dynamic Worker, which suits untrusted agent browsing. The catch: Dynamic Workers require a Workers Paid plan, and the project labels itself experimental.

Compatibility is the clever part. Kitesurf exposes a Chrome DevTools Protocol endpoint, so Puppeteer clients can connect over a WebSocket and call page.goto() or page.screenshot(). Developers can also use chrome://inspect or the DevTools frontend. But Cloudflare warns it is not a full Chrome implementation, so some DevTools features will not work yet.

The stack is Rust and WebAssembly built with Bazel, with pnpm and Node 22 for local tooling. Blitz supplies HTML parsing, DOM, layout and painting; the repo vendors Rust crates and pins toolchains. Local development runs through wrangler dev on port 8787, with health and CDP discovery endpoints. First builds compile the Rust core and are slow, then reuse Bazel cache.

DevTools support has two modes. By default the frontend comes from Google's hosted chrome-devtools-frontend, which only connects to 127.0.0.1 and prompts for permission. A --config=devtools Bazel build bundles a prebuilt Chromium DevTools frontend, required for deployed engines and heavier on first download. The repo exposes test, lint, format and e2e scripts through pnpm.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Kitesurf points to a cheaper, more granular substrate for agentic browsing: per-page isolated Workers at the edge instead of fleets of Chrome containers. That could lower cost and improve isolation for agents that visit untrusted pages, and CDP compatibility reduces switching costs. For developers, it is a useful experimental target for Puppeteer-style automation and a showcase for Rust/WASM rendering, but not yet a drop-in Chrome replacement; expect gaps in fidelity, JavaScript coverage and DevTools. For regular users, the near-term effect is indirect: more AI agents may browse and screenshot pages server-side, raising familiar questions about consent, bot traffic, rendering accuracy and abuse. Production adoption should wait for maturity and pricing clarity.
report.tools: Watch the Cloudflare/kitesurf repo, Dioxus Blitz for the Rust HTML/CSS rendering core, and Dioxus for the broader Rust UI ecosystem. Try puppeteer-core against the CDP endpoint, wrangler for local Workers development, and Bazelisk for the Bazel build. Cloudflare Dynamic Workers docs are essential because paid-plan isolation is a dependency. For comparisons, watch Puppeteer, Playwright and Chrome DevTools Protocol tooling.
